abstract: Resolving the genetic basis of insecticide resistance in Anopheles funestus has been limited both by the historic difficulty of germline transformation in this species and by the confounding genetic and metabolic background present in field populations. The A296S resistance-to-dieldrin (Rdl) mutation provides an informative proof-of-principle case because it has persisted at high frequency in African vector populations long after the withdrawal of dieldrin. Here, we used a marker-less CRISPR/Cas9 homology-directed repair strategy to introduce the A296S mutation in isolation into the insecticide-susceptible FANG strain of An. funestus. WHO tube bioassays were used to quantify resistance across different dieldrin exposure regimes and to assess cross-resistance to other insecticides, while larval development and adult longevity assays were used to evaluate life-history effects. A296S alone was sufficient to confer strong dieldrin resistance. Resistance was context-dependent: homozygous resistance remained robust at higher exposures, whereas heterozygote protection declined with increasing toxic load. No operationally relevant cross-resistance was detected to DDT or pyrethroids. The mutation imposed a modest, recessive delay in larval development, with no detectable reduction in adult longevity and no clear net disadvantage across the life-history traits measured. This study provides the first in vivo functional validation of an insecticide resistance mutation in An. funestus. By isolating A296S on a defined susceptible background, it provides a quantitative baseline for the effect of a single target-site mutation and offers new insight into how stage-specific fitness effects may contribute to the long-term persistence of resistance alleles in natural populations.
